response.text:
Concluding Remarks

The writer has often been inquired of whether this narrative is a true one; and to these inquiries she will give one general answer. The separate incidents are, to a very great extent, authentic—occurring, many of them, either under her own observation, or that of her personal friends. Characters the counterpart of almost all here introduced have been observed; many sayings are word for word as heard, or reported.

The personal appearance of Eliza, and the character ascribed to her, are sketches drawn from life. The incorruptible fidelity, piety, and honesty of Uncle Tom had more than one development to her personal knowledge. Some of the most deeply tragic and romantic, some of the most terrible incidents, have also their parallels in reality. The incident of the mother’s crossing the Ohio on the ice is a well-known fact. The story of “old Prue” fell under the observation of the writer’s brother, then collecting-clerk to a large mercantile house in New Orleans. From the same source was derived the character of the planter Legree. Of him her brother thus wrote, after visiting his plantation: “He actually made me feel of his fist, which was like a blacksmith’s hammer, or a nodule of iron, telling me that it was ‘calloused with knocking down niggers.’ When I left the plantation, I drew a long breath, and felt as if I had escaped from an ogre’s den.”

That the tragical fate of Tom also has too many times had its parallel, there are living witnesses to testify. Let it be remembered that in all southern states it is a principle of jurisprudence that no person of colored lineage can testify in a suit against a white; it will be easy to see that such a case may occur, wherever there is a man whose passions outweigh his interests, and a slave who has manhood or principle enough to resist his will. There is, actually, nothing to protect the slave’s life but the _character_ of the master. Facts too shocking to be contemplated occasionally force their way to the public ear; and the comment often heard is more shocking than the thing itself: “Very likely such cases may now and then occur, but they are no sample of general practice.” If the laws of New England were so arranged that a master could _now and then_ torture an apprentice to death, would it be received with equal composure? This injustice is an _inherent_ one in the slave system,—it cannot exist without it.

The public and shameless sale of beautiful mulatto and quadroon girls has acquired a notoriety from the incidents following the capture of the Pearl. We extract from the speech of Hon. Horace Mann, counsel for the defendants. He speaks of seventy-six persons who attempted, in 1848, to escape from the District of Columbia. “Elizabeth Russel was one of them. She immediately fell into the slave-trader’s fangs, and was doomed for the New Orleans market. They offered eighteen hundred dollars to redeem her; but the fiend of a slave-trader was inexorable. She was despatched to New Orleans; but, when about half way there, God had mercy on her, and smote her with death. There were two girls named Edmundson in the same company. When about to be sent to the same market, an older sister went to the shambles, to plead with the wretch who owned them. He bantered her, telling what fine dresses and fine furniture they would have. ‘Yes,’ she said, ‘that may do very well in this life, but what will become of them in the next?’ They too were sent to New Orleans; but were afterwards redeemed, at an enormous ransom, and brought back.” Is it not plain, from this, that the histories of Emmeline and Cassy may have many counterparts?

Justice, too, obliges the author to state that the fairness and generosity attributed to St. Clare are not without a parallel. A few years since, a young southern gentleman was in Cincinnati, with a favorite servant who had been his attendant from a boy. The young man secured his own freedom and fled to the protection of a Quaker. The owner, indignant, visited the Quaker; but, being possessed of uncommon candor, was soon quieted by his arguments. He immediately told the Quaker that, if his slave would, to his own face, say that it was his desire to be free, he would liberate him. An interview was procured; and Nathan was asked by his young master whether he had ever had any reason to complain of his treatment, in any respect.

“No, Mas’r,” said Nathan; “you’ve always been good to me.”

“Well, then, why do you want to leave me?”

“Mas’r may die, and then who get me?—I’d rather be a free man.”

After some deliberation, the young master replied, “Nathan, in your place, I think I should feel very much so, myself. You are free.”

He immediately made him out free papers; deposited a sum in the hands of the Quaker, to be used in assisting him to start in life; and left a sensible, kind letter of advice. That letter was for some time in the writer’s hands. The author hopes she has done justice to that nobility, generosity, and humanity which, in many cases, characterize individuals at the South. Such instances save us from utter despair of our kind. But—are such characters _common_, anywhere?

For many years, the author avoided all reading upon the subject of slavery, as too painful, and one which advancing light would certainly live down. But, since the act of 1850, when she heard, with surprise and consternation, Christian and humane people recommending the remanding of fugitives into slavery as a duty, she could only think, These men and Christians cannot know what slavery is; if they did, such a question could never be open. Hence a desire to exhibit it in a _living dramatic reality_. She has endeavored to show it fairly, in its best and its worst phases. In its _best_ aspect, she has, perhaps, been successful; but, oh! who shall say what yet remains untold in that valley and shadow of death that lies the other side?

To you, generous, noble-minded men and women of the South,—you, whose virtue and magnanimity are the greater for the severer trial,—to you is her appeal. Have you not, in your own secret souls, felt that there are woes and evils in this accursed system far beyond what is here shadowed? Can it be otherwise? Is _man_ ever to be trusted with wholly irresponsible power? And does not the slave system, by denying the slave all legal right of testimony, make every individual owner an irresponsible despot? If there is, as we admit, a public sentiment among you, men of honor and humanity, is there not also another public sentiment among the ruffian, the brutal and debased? And cannot the ruffian, the brutal, the debased, by slave law, own as many slaves as the best and purest? Are the honorable and compassionate the majority anywhere?

The slave-trade is now, by American law, considered piracy. But a slave-trade, as systematic as ever on the coast of Africa, is an inevitable attendant and result of American slavery. And its heart-break and its horrors, can they be told? The writer has given but a faint shadow of the anguish and despair that, at this moment, rive thousands of hearts, shatter thousands of families, and drive a helpless and sensitive race to frenzy. There are those living who know the mothers whom this traffic has driven to the murder of their children, and themselves to seek in death a shelter from woes more dreaded than death. Nothing of tragedy can equal the frightful reality of scenes daily acting on our shores, beneath the shadow of American law and the shadow of the cross of Christ.

And now, men and women of America, is this a thing to be trifled with, apologized for, and passed over in silence? Farmers of Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Vermont, Connecticut,—strong-hearted sailors and ship-owners of Maine,—brave and generous men of New York, farmers of rich Ohio, and ye of the wide prairie states,—answer, is this a thing for you to protect and countenance? And you, mothers of America,—you who have learned, by the cradles of your own children, to love and feel for all mankind,—by the sacred love you bear your child; by your joy in his beautiful, spotless infancy; by the motherly pity with which you guide his growing years; by the anxieties of his education; by the prayers you breathe for his soul’s eternal good;—I beseech you, pity the mother who has all your affections, and not one legal right to protect, guide, or educate, the child of her bosom! By the sick hour of your child; by those dying eyes you can never forget; by those last cries that wrung your heart when you could neither help nor save; by the desolation of that empty cradle, that silent nursery,—pity those mothers constantly made childless by the American slave-trade! And say, mothers of America, is this a thing to be defended, sympathized with, passed over in silence?

Do you say that the people of the free state have nothing to do with it? Would to God it were true! But it is not. The people of the free states have defended, encouraged, and participated; and are more guilty for it before God than the South, in that they have not the apology of education or custom. If the mothers of the free states had felt as they should, the sons of the free states would not have been the holders, and, proverbially, the hardest masters of slaves; would not have connived at the extension of slavery; would not trade the souls and bodies of men as an equivalent to money, in their dealings. There are multitudes of slaves temporarily owned and sold again by merchants in northern cities; and shall the whole guilt fall only on the South? Northern men, northern mothers, northern Christians, have something more to do than denounce their brethren; they have to look to the evil among themselves.

But what can any individual do? There is one thing every individual can do,—they can see to it that _they feel right_. An atmosphere of sympathetic influence encircles every human being; and the man or woman who _feels_ strongly, healthily and justly, on the great interests of humanity, is a constant benefactor. See, then, to your sympathies in this matter! And, Christian men and women of the North, you have another power; you can _pray!_ You pray for the heathen abroad; pray also for the heathen at home. And pray for those distressed Christians whose chance of religious improvement is an accident of trade and sale; for whom any adherence to the morals of Christianity is, in many cases, an impossibility, unless there be given, from above, the courage and grace of martyrdom.

But, still more. On the shores of our free states are emerging the poor, shattered remnants of families,—men and women escaped, by providences, from the surges of slavery,—feeble in knowledge, and, in many cases, infirm in moral constitution, from a system which confounds every principle of Christianity and morality. They come to seek refuge among you,—education, knowledge, Christianity. What do you owe to these poor unfortunates, oh Christians? Does not every American Christian owe to the African race some effort at reparation for the wrongs the American nation has brought upon them? Shall the doors of churches and school-houses be shut upon them? Shall states arise and shake them out? Shall the church of Christ hear in silence the taunt thrown at them; and, by her silence, encourage the cruelty that would chase them from our borders?

Do you say, “We don’t want them here; let them go to Africa”? That the providence of God has provided a refuge in Africa is a great fact; but that is no reason why the church of Christ should throw off that responsibility to this outcast race which her profession demands. To fill up Liberia with an ignorant, inexperienced, half-barbarized race, just escaped from chains, would be only to prolong, for ages, the struggle which attends the inception of new enterprises. Let the church of the north receive these sufferers in the spirit of Christ; receive them to the educating advantages of Christian republican society and schools, until they have attained somewhat of moral and intellectual maturity, and then assist them in their passage to those shores, where they may put in practice the lessons learned in America.

There is a body of men at the north, comparatively small, who have been doing this; and, as the result, this country has seen examples of men, formerly slaves, rapidly acquiring property, reputation, education. Talent has been developed, which, considering the circumstances, is remarkable; and, for moral traits of honesty, kindness, tenderness of feeling,—for heroic efforts and self-denials endured for the ransom of brethren and friends yet in slavery,—they have been remarkable to a surprising degree.

The writer has lived, for many years, on the frontier-line of slave states, and has had great opportunities of observation among those who formerly were slaves. They have been in her family as servants; and, in default of any other school to receive them, she has, in many cases, had them instructed in a family school, with her own children. She has also the testimony of missionaries among the fugitives in Canada, in coincidence with her own experience; and her deductions, with regard to the capabilities of the race, are encouraging in the highest degree. The first desire of the emancipated slave, generally, is for _education_. There is nothing that they are not willing to give or do to have their children instructed; they are remarkably intelligent and quick to learn. The results of schools, founded for them in Cincinnati, fully establish this.

On the authority of Professor C. E. Stowe, then of Lane Seminary, Ohio, the following among emancipated slaves in Cincinnati show the capability of the race. “B——. Furniture maker; twenty years in the city; worth ten thousand dollars. C——. Full black; stolen from Africa; sold in New Orleans; free fifteen years; a farmer; owns several farms in Indiana; worth fifteen or twenty thousand dollars. K——. Full black; dealer in real estate; worth thirty thousand dollars; paid eighteen hundred dollars for his family. G——. Full black; coal dealer; about thirty; worth eighteen thousand dollars; paid for himself twice, being once defrauded to the amount of sixteen hundred dollars. W——. Three-fourths black; barber and waiter; from Kentucky; nineteen years free; paid for self and family over three thousand dollars. G. D——. Three-fourths black; white-washer; from Kentucky; nine years free; recently died, aged sixty; worth six thousand dollars.” Professor Stowe adds that, with all these except G——, he had been, for some years, personally acquainted.

The writer well remembers an aged colored washerwoman in her father’s family. The daughter of this woman married a slave. By industry and thrift, and persevering self-denial, she raised nine hundred dollars for her husband’s freedom, paying it, as she raised it, into the hands of his master. She yet wanted a hundred dollars of the price, when he died. She never recovered any of the money.

These are but few facts, among multitudes, to show the self-denial, energy, patience, and honesty, which the slave has exhibited in freedom. Let it be remembered that these individuals have bravely succeeded in conquering for themselves comparative wealth and social position, in the face of every disadvantage and discouragement. Nor are these instances confined to Ohio. In all states we see men, but yesterday burst from shackles, who, by a self-educating force, have risen to highly respectable stations. Pennington, among clergymen, Douglas and Ward, among editors, are well known instances. If this persecuted race, with every discouragement, have done thus much, how much more if the Christian church would act towards them in the spirit of her Lord!

This is an age when nations are trembling and convulsed. A mighty influence is abroad, surging and heaving the world, as with an earthquake. And is America safe? Every nation that carries in its bosom great and unredressed injustice has in it the elements of this last convulsion. For what is this power thus rousing, in all nations and languages, those groanings that cannot be uttered, for man’s freedom and equality? O, Church of Christ, read the signs of the times! Is not this power the spirit of Him whose kingdom is yet to come, and whose will to be done on earth as it is in heaven? But who may abide the day of his appearing? “for that day shall burn as an oven: and he shall appear as a swift witness against those that oppress the hireling in his wages, the widow and the fatherless, and that _turn aside the stranger in his right_: and he shall break in pieces the oppressor.”

Are not these dread words for a nation bearing in her bosom so mighty an injustice? Christians! every time that you pray that the kingdom of Christ may come, can you forget that prophecy associates, in dread fellowship, the _day of vengeance_ with the year of his redeemed? A day of grace is yet held out to us. Both North and South have been guilty before God; and the _Christian church_ has a heavy account to answer. Not by combining together, to protect injustice and cruelty, and making a common capital of sin, is this Union to be saved,—but by repentance, justice and mercy; for, not surer is the eternal law by which the millstone sinks in the ocean, than that stronger law, by which injustice and cruelty shall bring on nations the wrath of Almighty God!
